strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing speech codec frame rates for speech language models while preserving semantic content. The 3-12.5 Hz controllable dynamic-rate setting is practically relevant for efficient AR speech generation.

The proposed system is technically coherent: ASR-guided semantic features, dynamic adjacent-frame merging, dual semantic/acoustic streams, FSQ/RVQ quantization, and frame unmerging are integrated into a complete codec pipeline.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The paper reports semantic reconstruction WER, acoustic quality metrics, bitrate/frame-rate comparisons, dynamic-rate ablations, component ablations, downstream TTS experiments, and audio understanding probing.

Results are compelling at low frame rates. In particular, the reported RVQ-1 WER at 6.25 Hz is much better than retrained DAC/DualCodec baselines, and ablations suggest dynamic frame allocation provides measurable gains over fixed-frame-rate variants.
The paper is mostly clear and includes useful implementation details, training settings, model sizes, loss weights, and appendices that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental in several components: dynamic token merging, ASR/SSL semantic guidance, dual-stream codecs, FSQ, and transformer bottlenecks all have close precedents. The novelty is mainly their combination and application below 10 Hz rather than a fundamentally new compression principle.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully settled. Several key low-frame-rate baselines are retrained by the authors after architectural modifications, and it is unclear whether they are equally optimized. Comparisons to open-source codecs also mix different training data, model sizes, bitrates, and objectives.

The bitrate and efficiency claims are somewhat under-specified. Dynamic tokens require length side information, and the codec relies on a large frozen ASR encoder plus a 216M-parameter trainable codec; computational cost, latency, and memory are not analyzed carefully enough for the claimed edge/adaptive-use motivation.
The frame-rate thresholds for 8.3 Hz and 6.25 Hz are selected based on trial runs on the test set, which weakens the cleanliness of the evaluation for controllable-rate claims.

The semantic gains may partly reflect dependence on a strong ASR model trained directly for transcription. This is useful engineering, but it narrows the scientific interpretation: the method may inherit ASR biases and may not generalize to multilingual, noisy, code-switched, or non-speech audio settings. The paper only evaluates English speech for the main codec experiments.

The TTS subjective evaluation is relatively small and the MOS confidence intervals overlap substantially across systems, so the claims of perceptual superiority should be toned down. The strongest TTS setting also uses a 50 Hz NAR decoder, so the downstream generation result does not by itself prove that very low frame rates suffice for high-quality full speech synthesis.
Reproducibility is promising but incomplete at review time: code is described as supplementary/future open source, while demos appear to have a missing or blank URL in the extracted manuscript.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing speech codec frame rates for speech language models while preserving semantic content.
The dynamic frame-rate idea is well motivated, and the use of ASR features to guide merging is intuitive and technically plausible.
The paper includes a fairly broad set of automatic evaluations, including semantic WER, acoustic metrics, ablations, open-source codec comparisons, and downstream TTS/audio-understanding experiments.
Results suggest clear gains over retrained DAC/DualCodec variants at very low frame rates, especially for RVQ-1 semantic preservation.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines pretrained ASR features, adjacent-frame similarity merging, FSQ/RVQ, and transformer bottlenecks, all of which are natural extensions of recent low-frame-rate and dynamic-tokenization work.

The evaluation is not fully convincing for a top-tier claim. Most codec evidence is automatic, largely on clean English LibriSpeech-style data, with no substantial subjective listening test for codec reconstruction quality.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: FlexiCodec uses a large frozen 234M-parameter ASR encoder trained on 300k hours plus 216M trainable parameters, while many baselines are smaller or adapted by the authors rather than taken from optimized low-frame-rate designs.
The paper tunes frame-rate thresholds using trial runs on the test set, which weakens the validity of reported 8.3Hz and 6.25Hz operating points.
The claim of controllability down to 3Hz is overstated: at 3Hz the reported RVQ-1 WER is 51.5%, so the setting appears largely unusable for semantic preservation.

The TTS validation is underdeveloped relative to the claims: subjective evaluation uses only 10 audios per model and is relegated to the appendix, while comparisons may conflate codec quality with system/training differences.
Reproducibility is incomplete: demos and model release links appear blank or deferred, and the system is large and expensive to train, making independent verification difficult.

The paper does not adequately analyze practical costs such as ASR encoder latency, memory, side information for dynamic lengths, streaming limitations, or robustness to multilingual/noisy/out-of-domain speech.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: FlexiCodec targets an important bottleneck in speech language models by reducing codec frame rates below 10Hz while preserving semantic information.
The dynamic frame-rate design is technically well motivated and reasonably novel for low-frame-rate neural audio codecs, with interpretable ASR-feature-guided merging and inference-time rate control.

Empirical results are strong: the paper compares against retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines at matched very low frame rates, and shows especially large gains in RVQ-1 semantic preservation at 6.25Hz.

The evaluation is broad, covering semantic WER, acoustic quality metrics, bitrate/frame-rate comparisons with many open-source codecs, ablations, ASR probing, downstream TTS, and audio understanding tasks.
Ablations support the main design choices, including dynamic frame rate, ASR features, transformer-based merging/unmerging, and FSQ quantization.
The downstream TTS results are practically compelling, showing competitive quality with substantial autoregressive speedups.
weaknesses: The system relies on a large frozen ASR encoder trained on 300k hours, and the paper could better separate the contribution of the codec architecture from the advantage conferred by this strong pretrained semantic model.

The efficiency and bitrate claims are somewhat complicated by the large total model size, the ASR encoder cost, and the need to transmit/store frame-length attributes; it is not fully clear whether all overhead is included consistently in bitrate comparisons.

The frame-rate thresholds for 12.5Hz, 8.3Hz, and 6.25Hz are selected from trial runs on the test set, which raises a mild evaluation hygiene concern; a validation set should be used for this calibration.

Generality is still limited: training and main evaluation are English speech only, with no multilingual, code-switched, noisy real-world, music, or streaming evaluation despite claims about broader codec utility.
The subjective TTS evaluation is relatively small, and several TTS baseline numbers are borrowed from official results or not fully comparable in hardware/runtime setup.

The controllable-rate claim is strongest in the 6.25-12.5Hz range; although the method can produce about 3Hz tokens, the reported semantic WER at that rate is very high, so the practical usefulness of the lowest rates remains unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reducing speech codec frame rates for speech LMs/TTS while preserving semantic content and reconstruction quality.

The dynamic-rate formulation is practically useful: one trained codec can trade frame rate against quality at inference time, and the frame-length attributes make the representation explicit and usable downstream.

Empirical evaluation is broad. The paper reports semantic WER, acoustic metrics, bitrate-controlled codec comparisons, ablations, TTS experiments, speed measurements, out-of-domain English tests, multilingual tests, and audio-understanding probes.
The main low-frame-rate results are compelling: FlexiCodec substantially improves RVQ-1 semantic preservation over retrained DAC/DualCodec at 6.25Hz, while maintaining reasonable acoustic quality.

Ablations are informative and mostly support the design: ASR features are the dominant contributor, dynamic frame rate adds further gains, and transformer merging/unmerging mainly improves acoustic quality.
The paper is generally clear about architecture, training setup, parameter counts, and limitations, including English-centric training and lack of streaming support.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental. The strongest gains appear to come from replacing SSL features with frozen ASR features; the dynamic merging itself is a simple cosine-threshold heuristic with modest additional improvements over a strong ASR-feature fixed-rate baseline.
The claim of controllable frame rates down to 3Hz is only weakly supported: at 3Hz the reported WER is very poor, so practical usefulness at that regime is questionable.

Thresholds for target frame rates are selected from trial runs on the test set, which risks test-set tuning. A held-out validation procedure would make the rate-control and performance claims cleaner.

The codec evaluation relies heavily on objective proxy metrics, especially ASR WER and learned MOS predictors. There is no subjective listening evaluation for codec reconstruction quality, despite this being central to an audio codec paper.

TTS evaluation is useful but not fully isolating the codec contribution: the strongest TTS system uses a 50Hz NAR decoder, so the final audio quality is not solely due to low-frame-rate FlexiCodec tokens. Subjective testing is also small, with only 10 audios per system.

Comparisons to baselines are somewhat uneven: some baselines are retrained by the authors, others use official checkpoints, several lack RVQ-1 decoding, and model sizes/training data differ substantially. This makes some state-of-the-art claims less definitive.
The method is heavy for a codec: the full system includes a frozen 234M ASR model and 216M trainable parameters, which weakens efficiency claims despite good RTF measurements on GPU.

Generalization remains limited. RVQ-1 semantic performance collapses on several non-English languages before fine-tuning, so the approach is currently English-centric despite claims about broader utility.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as presented: audio demo and code links appear blank, and several implementation details for exact baseline retraining and test-set threshold selection would need code to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: reducing codec frame rate for speech/audio language models while preserving semantic information and reconstruction quality.

FlexiCodec has a coherent technical design combining ASR-feature guidance, dual-stream encoding, dynamic frame merging, FSQ semantic quantization, and frame unmerging; the method is described at a reasonable level of detail.

The empirical section is fairly broad, including comparisons at 12.5, 8.3, and 6.25 Hz, ablations of dynamic frame rate and other components, bitrate comparisons against many open-source codecs, TTS experiments, audio-understanding probes, speed measurements, and OOD/multilingual tests.
The reported semantic preservation results on LibriSpeech-test-clean are strong, especially the low RVQ-1 WER at 6.25 Hz compared with retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines.
The ablations usefully reveal that ASR features are the dominant factor, while dynamic frame rate, transformer modules, and FSQ provide additional incremental gains.
weaknesses: The central novelty is weaker than the presentation suggests. Much of the headline improvement appears to come from replacing SSL features with a strong frozen ASR encoder trained on 300k hours, rather than from the dynamic-rate algorithm itself. The dynamic-rate gains over fixed-rate FlexiCodec are real but comparatively modest.

The evaluation has potential test-set selection issues: the paper states that tau values for target frame rates were determined from trial runs on the test set, which undermines the cleanliness of the reported LibriSpeech results.

The comparison to baselines is not fully convincing. Retrained DAC/DualCodec variants may not be optimized as carefully as the proposed model, and several open-source baselines differ greatly in training data, supervision, model size, bitrate accounting, and supported token interfaces. This makes broad state-of-the-art claims too strong.

The semantic metrics are heavily ASR-centric while the model itself is ASR-feature-assisted. WER of reconstructed audio is important, but the paper needs stronger evidence that the tokens are generally useful beyond matching ASR behavior, especially for downstream speech/audio LMs.

The claimed efficiency benefits are not cleanly demonstrated. FlexiCodec uses a large 216M trainable codec plus a frozen 234M ASR model and unmerges to a fixed 12.5 Hz decoder path; codec RTF is constant across frame rates, so the practical runtime advantage is mainly downstream and only partially validated.

The TTS results are relegated to the appendix and are not fully isolating the codec contribution. Baselines include borrowed official results, subjective evaluation is small, and the TTS system introduces architecture choices beyond the codec itself.

Reproducibility is a concern: the abstract contains blank demo/code links in the extracted manuscript, and the work requires substantial training compute and large datasets. Important details for retraining baselines and reproducing subjective evaluations remain insufficient.
Generalization is mixed. The model performs poorly for RVQ-1 semantic preservation on non-English languages without fine-tuning, which weakens broad claims about robust semantic tokenization.

The paper overclaims in several places, e.g. “state-of-the-art audio quality” and “high-quality reconstructible audio below 10 Hz,” despite relying mostly on proxy metrics and lacking a dedicated subjective codec-quality evaluation.
Ethical and misuse considerations are underdeveloped for a speech codec/TTS-oriented system, particularly around voice cloning, synthetic speech misuse, consent, and watermarking or detection.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper tackles very low-frame-rate neural speech tokenization, a practically important bottleneck for speech LMs and TTS, and proposes a coherent combination of ASR-guided semantic encoding, dynamic frame merging, and frame-rate controllability.

The empirical results are strong. FlexiCodec substantially improves RVQ-1 semantic preservation at 6.25Hz over retrained DAC/DualCodec baselines, while maintaining competitive acoustic quality across bitrate regimes.

The evaluation is broad and unusually complete: codec metrics, bitrate comparisons, ablations, ASR probing, TTS downstream experiments, audio-understanding tasks, efficiency measurements, and OOD/multilingual analyses are all included.

The ablations support the main design choices. In particular, the paper separates the effects of ASR features, dynamic frame rate, transformer merge/unmerge modules, and FSQ, making the source of gains reasonably convincing.
The dynamic-rate analysis is insightful: the correlation with phoneme rate and qualitative TIMIT visualizations make the merging behavior interpretable rather than just an engineering trick.
The method appears practically relevant for TTS, with competitive quality and meaningful autoregressive speedups at lower frame rates.
weaknesses: A central part of the method depends on a large frozen supervised ASR model trained on 300k hours. This complicates the framing as a general codec and means some gains may come from importing strong ASR supervision rather than from the codec architecture alone.

The paper states that frame-rate thresholds were selected via trial runs on the test set. Even if only used to match target average rates, this is poor evaluation hygiene and should be moved to a validation set.

The claim of continuous controllability from 3Hz to 12.5Hz is only partially demonstrated. Most core evaluations focus on 6.25, 8.3, and 12.5Hz, with very low rates around 3-4.5Hz showing large WER degradation.
Subjective TTS evaluation is relatively small: six experts rating only 10 samples per system gives limited statistical power, especially since subjective quality is a key downstream claim.

Comparisons to open-source codecs are broad but heterogeneous: baselines differ in training data, supervision, intended domain, model size, and support for RVQ-1 decoding, which makes some table-level wins harder to interpret cleanly.

The method is not streaming and is trained mainly on English; multilingual results show severe RVQ-1 semantic failures before language-specific fine-tuning, limiting the immediate generality of the approach.

Reproducibility is not fully clear from the manuscript text: the abstract has blank demo/code links, and reproducing the system requires large-scale training resources and a specific pretrained ASR feature extractor.
